source_read: Publisher HTML (Springer Nature Link, Harm Reduct J 18:30, open access), read in full in the built-in browser: all text sections, Funding and Competing interests; Figs. 1-3 checked on the full-size images (/figures/1-3), including the strip photographs. Additional file 1 (DOCX download with the remaining strip images, including the temperature experiment) not opened.

claims.note: The 4 °C result is as stated: diphenhydramine tablet and capsule solutions at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL all read positive (control band only) when the strips were run at 4 °C. Wording: 'with no fentanyl-free cold solution tested' is imprecise, since every diphenhydramine solution was itself fentanyl-free; what is missing is a cold blank without any drug (and a cold fentanyl solution), so whether cold alone removes the test band cannot be told. The number of strips per cold condition is not given, and the cold-run images are only in Additional file 1. The same experiment at 40 °C gave the same readings as at 25 °C, a short in-run heat result the 'Heat and age' sentence does not mention. The authors' general statement that the test band does not react properly at or below 4 °C goes beyond what was tested (one drug, one temperature below room temperature).

anchors.extracted: Strips run with diphenhydramine tablets and capsules at 4 °C, 25 °C and 40 °C, at 4, 2 and 1 mg/mL, left 5 min to develop in each condition. At 25 and 40 °C: tablets false positive at 4 mg/mL only, capsules at 4 and 2 mg/mL, both negative at 1 mg/mL. At 4 °C every strip read positive (control band only); authors conclude the test band does not react properly at or below 4 °C. No water blank or fentanyl control in the cold; strip numbers not stated; images in Additional file 1.
One brand (BTNX Rapid Response, 20 ng/mL), two lots (D808009, DOA903194), kept sealed until immediately before use; which lot was used for which experiment is not stated.

claims.overstatement: The claim gives '25 ng/mL by eye' without the reading rule it depends on. In Fig. 1 the pictured strips at 50 and 25 ng/mL both show a faint but visible test band, which the reading rule the paper itself states (any pink band in the test area means fentanyl not present) would read as negative; the lowest pictured concentration with no visible band is 63 ng/mL. The 25 ng/mL figure therefore counts a faint band as positive, like the authors' rule in Bergh et al., and should say so (for example: '25 ng/mL by eye when a faint test band was counted as positive; about 63 ng/mL under the makers' rule, from the published images').
claims.note: Five strips at each of 125, 100, 83, 63, 50, 25 and 5 ng/mL confirmed. At 25 ng/mL the test band measured 1152 counts (n = 5, SD 72), and this faint band's intensity became the image-analysis threshold. The paper does not say how many of the five 25 ng/mL strips were read positive by eye. The abstract and conclusion say the strips detect fentanyl 'to the specified limit of detection' (20 ng/mL), which their own result (25 ng/mL, with a visible band) does not quite show. The Discussion's claim that over-dilution is not a likely problem (50 ng/mL from 0.5 mg in a 10-L bucket) is an untested extrapolation.

anchors.extracted: Certified fentanyl standard, methanol evaporated, diluted in deionized water from 1 mg/mL to 5 ng/mL; five strips at each of 125, 100, 83, 63, 50, 25 and 5 ng/mL.

Limit of detection by eye 25 ng/mL; test-band intensity at 25 ng/mL 1152 counts (n = 5, SD 72), described as consistent with the 20 ng/mL on the packaging and used as the 'fentanyl threshold line'. Plot: about 2500 counts at 5 ng/mL, about 850 at 50, about 600 at 63, about 250 at 125 ng/mL.

anchors.locator: Fig. 1 (strip photographs a-g) against Methods › Fentanyl test strips, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Strips at 125, 100, 83 and 63 ng/mL show no test band; strips at 50 and 25 ng/mL show a faint but visible test band; 5 ng/mL a strong band. The Methods state that any pink band in the test area indicates fentanyl is not present.
Authors: strips detect fentanyl to the specified limit; over-dilution unlikely to matter because 0.5 mg of fentanyl in 10 L (50 ng/mL) would still be detected. Not tested.

claims.note: Numbers match: by eye no test band above about 2 mg/mL for methamphetamine, MDMA and both diphenhydramine products; by image analysis critical concentrations 1 (capsules), 1.5 (methamphetamine), 2 (MDMA) and 2.5 mg/mL (tablets); cocaine, alprazolam, gabapentin and naloxone-buprenorphine negative by eye at 20 mg/mL; one strip per dilution; seized methamphetamine, MDMA and cocaine (one sample each, purity confirmed but not reported) and retail or coroner-sourced medicines, so concentrations are of weighed material. Editors' calculation recomputed: 25 mg diphenhydramine HCl in a 240 mg capsule and a 250 mg tablet gives 0.104 mg/mL at 1 mg/mL of capsule material and 0.25 mg/mL at 2.5 mg/mL of tablet material, the same as the card's 'about 0.10 and 0.25'. Qualifications: 1.5 mg/mL is not a tested concentration (the dilution list goes from 2 to 1 mg/mL; Fig. 3 shows methamphetamine below the threshold at 2 and above it at 1, so 1.5 is interpolated); the capsule point at 1 mg/mL and the MDMA point at 2 mg/mL sit on the threshold line; the threshold is the intensity of the faint band left by 25 ng/mL fentanyl, so image analysis counts as positive some strips whose faint band the makers' rule would read as negative; in the temperature experiment the capsule solution at 1 mg/mL read negative at room temperature although 1 mg/mL is called the critical concentration; and the 4% difference in diphenhydramine content between capsules and tablets cannot explain the 2.5-fold difference the authors attribute to fillers, which points to single-strip variation. Within this study the lowest false-positive concentration is about 40,000 times the fentanyl limit (1 mg/mL against 25 ng/mL), outside the claim's cross-study '1,000 to 25,000'.

anchors.extracted: Diphenhydramine tablets and capsules (25 mg) bought in a grocery store; alprazolam tablets, gabapentin capsules and naloxone-buprenorphine tablets from a county coroner's office (from accidental overdose deaths), identity by pill databases and LC-MS; cocaine HCl, methamphetamine and MDMA from a county forensic laboratory as independent seizures, identity and purity confirmed by FTIR and GC-MS (purity not reported).
20 mg of each interferent dissolved to 20 mg/mL, then diluted to 10, 6.7, 4, 2.5, 2, 1, 0.67, 0.50, 0.40, 0.33, 0.29, 0.25, 0.22 and 0.20 mg/mL; one strip per dilution; photographed at 5 min.

anchors.locator: Results › Interference study, 2nd paragraph; Figs. 2 and 3
anchors.extracted: By eye: cocaine, alprazolam, gabapentin and naloxone-buprenorphine negative even at 20 mg/mL; methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine capsules and tablets lost the test band above about 2 mg/mL. By image analysis against the 25 ng/mL fentanyl band intensity: critical concentrations 1 mg/mL (capsules), 2.5 (tablets), 1.5 (methamphetamine) and 2 mg/mL (MDMA); deionized and tap-water blanks and cocaine stayed well above the threshold.

Sub-graph points at 4, 2.5, 2, 1 and 0.67 mg/mL: methamphetamine below threshold at 2, above at 1 (no 1.5 mg/mL solution in Fig. 2 or the Methods); MDMA at 2 mg/mL and capsules at 1 mg/mL lie on the threshold; tablets below at 2.5, above at 2. Error bars are described as SD of replicate measurements although the Methods give one strip per dilution.

Capsule average weight 240 mg (n = 3, SD 3), tablet 250 mg (n = 3, SD 4), both 25 mg diphenhydramine HCl; authors attribute the tablets' higher critical concentration to more filler. At room temperature the capsule solution read negative at 1 mg/mL and positive at 2 and 4 mg/mL.

Worked examples (5 mg methamphetamine in 1 mL would give 5 mg/mL and a false positive; 10 mL would give 0.5 mg/mL) and the recommended minimum dilution volume are reasoning from the laboratory curves, not tested on real residues or mixtures with fentanyl.

key_findings.correction: Keep the finding, but the note's open question can be settled from Fig. 1: the pictured strips at 50 ng/mL (e) and 25 ng/mL (f) both show a faint but visible test band, those at 63 ng/mL and above none, and 5 ng/mL a strong band. Under the reading rule the paper states, the pictured 25 ng/mL strip reads negative (lowest pictured concentration without a band: 63 ng/mL), so the 25 ng/mL limit by eye counts a faint band as positive, and the 1152-count threshold is the intensity of a visible band.
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 plot: about 2500 counts at 5 ng/mL, 1150 at 25, 850 at 50, 600 at 63, 550 at 83, 430 at 100 and 250 at 125 ng/mL.
Volumes and concentrations recomputed; Fig. 2 rows match the 15 steps (no 1.5 mg/mL row).

Fig. 3: cocaine at 20 mg/mL is about 1550 counts, roughly a third above the 1150 threshold, rising to about 4500 by 2 mg/mL, so 'well above' holds least at the top concentration. Alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone images are only in Additional file 1, not in Figs. 2-3.

Fig. 3 sub-graphs show the derivation the text omits: methamphetamine below the threshold at 2 mg/mL and above it at 1 mg/mL, so 1.5 is interpolated; MDMA at 2 mg/mL and capsules at 1 mg/mL sit on the line; tablets cross between 2.5 and 2 mg/mL. In Fig. 2 very faint traces are visible in some boxed cells (methamphetamine and MDMA at 10-2.5 mg/mL), so near-threshold readings by eye are ambiguous.
Editors' calculation recomputed: 25/240 x 1 = 0.104 and 25/250 x 2.5 = 0.25 mg/mL diphenhydramine HCl.

Wording of the note: the diphenhydramine solutions were themselves fentanyl-free; what is missing is a drug-free (water) blank and a fentanyl solution at 4 °C. Number of strips per condition not stated; images in Additional file 1.

reporting_issues.note: The sub-graph error bars are visible at 4, 2.5, 2, 1 and 0.67 mg/mL (Fig. 3).
Fig. 3: interpolated between 2 mg/mL (below threshold) and 1 mg/mL (above).

Confirmed by the images: the 25 and 50 ng/mL strips in Fig. 1 show a faint visible test band, so the threshold corresponds to a strip the stated rule reads as negative, and ImageJ calls are more liberal than the makers' rule.
Trace fentanyl cannot explain the retail diphenhydramine results, and Halifax et al. (2024) reproduce the methamphetamine and MDMA effect with pure standards.
As for key finding 7: 'fentanyl-free cold blank' should read drug-free (water) blank, since the diphenhydramine solutions were fentanyl-free.

risk_of_bias.note: Sample selection high, index test high, reference standard unclear, flow and timing unclear, overall high: agree. The index-test judgment is strengthened by Fig. 1 (threshold set at a visibly banded strip). For the reference standard, the editors' trace-fentanyl calculation applies to the seized stimulants only (about 0.001-0.0025% fentanyl by weight at 1-2.5 mg/mL, recomputed); it cannot explain the grocery-store diphenhydramine products.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. One addition: the abstract and Conclusion say the strips detect fentanyl 'to the specified limit of detection', but the 25 ng/mL result rests on a faint visible band that the stated rule reads as negative (Fig. 1), so even the paper's positive message on sensitivity is stronger than its images show.

missed: Fig. 1 strip images (faint visible test band at 25 and 50 ng/mL, none from 63 ng/mL up) settle the card's open question about the 25 ng/mL limit; under the makers' rule the pictured limit would be about 63 ng/mL. This qualifies any claim citing '25 ng/mL by eye'.

Figs. 2-3 show deionized- and tap-water blank strips alongside each dilution step (15 each in Fig. 2), all with strong test bands and far above the threshold in Fig. 3; the card's comparison field says only that tap water is missing from the Methods.

In-run heat: at 40 °C the diphenhydramine readings matched room temperature (Results › Interference study, 4th paragraph), the only heat result in this paper; relevant to the claim on strip ageing and heat.
